meta.title: Use of Laboratory Thermometer in Pharmaceutical Chemistry Laboratory

sections.purpose: To accurately measure temperatures during synthesis reactions, distillations, recrystallizations, and melting point determinations in pharmaceutical chemistry experiments.
sections.scope: Applicable to Pharmaceutical Chemistry laboratory for all temperature measurement operations including reaction monitoring, boiling point determination, and bath temperature verification.
procedure: Select the correct thermometer range: 0–100°C for water baths; 0–250°C for oil baths and high-temperature reactions; −20 to +50°C for cold bath monitoring.
Inspect the thermometer for liquid column continuity, cracks, and calibration marks.
For mercury thermometers with separated columns: gently warm the bulb to rejoin the column before use.
Immerse to the correct depth: partial-immersion thermometers have a ring mark (usually 76 mm); full-immersion thermometers must be immersed to the meniscus level.
Clamp the thermometer securely using a thermometer clamp on a retort stand — do not allow it to rest against the flask wall or bottom.
For distillation: position the thermometer bulb at the side-arm junction of the distillation flask — this gives the true vapour temperature.
Allow 2–3 minutes for equilibration before reading.
Read at eye level with the meniscus: top of column for mercury; bottom of meniscus for coloured spirit.
Record temperature to the nearest 0.1°C in the laboratory register.
Remove, allow to cool, clean with solvent, then distilled water, and store in protective case.
Calibrate annually at ice point (0°C) and steam point (100°C) against reference.
precautions: Never use mercury thermometers near open flames or in reactions that might superheat — mercury toxicity is severe.
Never use as a stirring rod — mechanical stress cracks the glass and releases toxic mercury.
Ensure correct immersion depth — partial vs. full immersion gives temperature errors of 1–5°C.
Place in the correct position for distillations — bulb at side-arm junction gives true vapour temperature, not flask liquid temperature.
Allow hot thermometers to cool before plunging into cold liquid — thermal shock causes breakage.
If mercury thermometer breaks: evacuate the area, do not vacuum up mercury — follow mercury spill protocol.
